connections.observation: `s001` records Socrates' downward movement (καταβαίνων) to the Piraeus. `s004` cites Socrates' image of old age as a road (ὁδόν) already traveled, asking whether it is rough or easy. The spatial descent is followed immediately by a metaphorical path whose character is unknown.

`s003` contrasts withering bodily pleasures with growing desires for λόγοι. `s005` names the specific bodily pleasures most old men long for: sex, drinking, feasting. `s006` records their lament that they were truly living then but not now. The withering described in `s003` is enacted in `s006` as a reported judgment of non-life.

`s007` presents Sophocles' image of escaping a raging, mad master (λυττῶντά τινα καὶ ἄγριον δεσπότην) and generalizes it to many mad masters (δεσποτῶν μαινομένων). `s018` uses μανείς (mad) for the friend who demands weapons back. The madness attributed to erotic desire in `s007` recurs in the counterexample testing justice.

`s008` records the dense clustering of αἰτία/αἴτιον as Cephalus refutes the accusation that old age causes misery. `s009` names the true single cause as τρόπος (character), not γῆρας. The concentration of cause-language in `s008` resolves into the explicit contrast of `s009`.

`s010` traces three generations of inheritance: grandfather, father, Cephalus—each παραλαμβάνων and either increasing, decreasing, or preserving. `s015` names Polemarchus κληρονόμος and records Cephalus παραδίδωμι τὸν λόγον. The wealth passed through generations in `s010` is paralleled by the argument handed over to the heir.

`s011` presents the triple analogy: poets love poems, fathers love children, money-makers love money—each as their own ἔργον. `s015` shows Cephalus handing over the λόγος to Polemarchus, named κληρονόμος. The analogy of fathers and children loving their creations is enacted when the father hands both wealth-succession and argument-succession to his son.

`s012` introduces μῦθοι about Hades that demand δίκη be paid there (ἐκεῖ). `s013` states these myths were previously laughed at (καταγελώμενοι τέως) but now twist the soul (στρέφουσιν τὴν ψυχήν). The myths cited in `s012` undergo the temporal reversal described in `s013`.

`s012` cites myths of Hades and judgment (δίκην διδόναι ἐκεῖ). `s014` contrasts κακῆς ἐλπίδος for the unjust with ἡδεῖα ἐλπίς for the just. The afterlife punishment in `s012` is the ground of the opposed hopes in `s014`.

`s013` records that the myths now twist the soul (στρέφουσιν τὴν ψυχήν) of the one who fears. `s016` shows Cephalus laughing (γελάσας) as he departs. The fear and twisting in `s013` is absent from Cephalus' own departure; his laugh occurs where another might experience στρέφειν.

`s002` records ἰέναι twice with δεῦρο: first a counterfactual negation, then an imperative for frequency. `s017` records ἀποδιδόναι appearing three times in the proposed definition and its counterexample. Both sequences use exact repetition within a short span to test and revise a condition.

`s010` cites παραλαμβάνω and καταλείπω across three generations of wealth. `s019` shows οὐσία recurring with forms of κτάομαι at each mention. The verbs of receiving and leaving in `s010` frame the substantive (οὐσία) that is moved.

`s015` records Cephalus handing over the λόγος (παραδίδωμι) and departing for the ἱερά. `s016` shows this departure enacted: he laughs (γελάσας) and goes toward the sacrifices (ᾔει πρὸς τὰ ἱερά). The stated intention in `s015` is completed in `s016`.

elements.context: καὶ γῆρας, ὦ Σώκρατες, καὶ νεότης

new_signals.observation: Forms of νέος/νεότης recur as youth is named explicitly in contrast to old age, and as the site of pleasures now lost.

elements.context: ἐν τῷ γήρᾳ πολλὴ εἰρήνη γίγνεται καὶ ἐλευθερία

new_signals.observation: εἰρήνη and ἐλευθερία are named together as what comes to be in old age when desires relax.

elements.context: ἂν μὲν γὰρ κόσμιοι καὶ εὔκολοι ὦσιν

new_signals.observation: κόσμιος appears first describing the character that makes old age moderate, then describing the man for whom wealth is most useful.

elements.context: χαίρω γε διαλεγόμενος τοῖς σφόδρα πρεσβύταις
εἴπερ γέ τι χρὴ Σιμωνίδῃ πείθεσθαι

new_signals.observation: Socrates states his pleasure in διαλέγεσθαι with the very old; at the close Polemarchus questions whether one should πείθεσθαι Simonides. The mode shifts from dialogue to persuasion/trust.

elements.context: εἴπερ γέ τι χρὴ Σιμωνίδῃ πείθεσθαι

new_signals.observation: Cephalus cites Pindar approvingly; Polemarchus questions whether to trust Simonides. Two named poets frame the close of Cephalus' speech.
